newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate rises, financial markets rally.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate rises, financial markets rally.

text.p: The nation's tight labour market slackened a bit in June as the unemployment rate rose to 5 percent and job growth slowed in the private sector, the government said on Thursday.

The Labour Department report sparked a rally on Wall Street as investors saw no evidence of looming inflationary pressures that might make Federal Reserve policy-makers regret their decision on Wednesday to hold interest rates steady.

"The picture painted by this and other data is clearly one of moderate growth and low inflation," economist Richard Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh said. "It's a perfect environment for financial markets and for static monetary policy."

After dropping to a near 24-year low of 4.8 percent in May, the jobless rate unexpectedly bounced back to 5 percent last month as the ranks of the unemployed rose to 6.8 million from 6.5 million, the department said. The number of job holders fell to 129.4 million from 129.6 million, it said.

The report contained other signs that the job market, while still tight, was slackening. The number of people seeking jobs for 27 weeks or longer -- the so-called long-term unemployed -- and the number of workers who left their jobs involuntarily both rose in June.

Although the department's survey can produce erratic data from month to month, Bureau of Labour Statistics Commissioner Katharine Abraham said the significance of the increase in the jobless rate should not be downplayed.
"It's statistically significant, but I'm not sure how economically meaningful it was," she told a news conference.
The Clinton administration said the report showed an economy moving at a slower but still healthy pace.

"Clearly, the economy is moving at a sustainable clip," Labour Secretary Alexis Herman said in a statement. "As we enter the month of July, the summer weather may be hot, but the nation's employment situation is very comfortable."

The department's more closely watched payroll survey showed the economy created 217,000 jobs in June, up from 166,000 in May. But in the private sector, job growth outside the farm sector slowed to 151,000 in June from 180,000 in May.

Economists said job growth overall in June was probably overstated by a statistical quirk in the seasonal adjustments that made it appear as if 49,000 jobs were added to state and local school payrolls.
The report, the government's first look at the health of the economy in June, followed other recent signs that growth was slowing from its rapid first quarter pace.

"It's still a very solid job market, but somewhat slacker in June," said economist Allen Sinai of Primark Decision Economics Inc. in Boston. "There's nothing really wrong with the U.S. economy or the job market. It actually is humming along almost ideally."

After the report, the Dow Jones industrial average jumped 100.43 points to close at a record 7,895.81, while the 30-year Treasury jumped more than a point, lowering its yield to 6.62 percent from 6.71 percent on Wednesday. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Fed policy-makers on Wednesday left short-term rates unchanged on growing signs the economy was slowing from its rapid 5.9 percent first-quarter growth rate. Many economists say second-quarter growth slowed to about a 2 percent rate.

With growth downshifting, AFL-CIO economist Tom Palley said the central bank should cut interest rates as "insurance" against a sharp slowdown, just as Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan called a March increase in short-term rates insurance against inflation.
"I don't think there's any indication across the board now of inflation," said Palley. "At the same time, there is an indication of a slowing -- though nothing worse than that."

Average hourly earnings last month rose by 4 cents, the same increase as in May, to $12.22, and were up just 3.5 percent over the past year. But the past year's gain still outpaced inflation and represents "real" wage growth.
The June payrolls increase included 58,000 new jobs in the retail sector, as well as gains of 11,000 in computer and data processing and 14,000 in engineering and management services.

In the manufacturing sector, where stocks of unsold goods are piling up and orders fell in two of the past three months, overtime and the average workweek slipped in June, but job growth rose slightly to 14,000 from 5,000 in May.
